pages.text: Watch: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America. Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory". On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire. There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love." The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope. He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/wear-and-tear-changes-measurable-pfas-levels-firefighter-hoods-gloves-and NEWS Wear and Tear Changes Measurable PFAS Levels in Firefighter Hoods, Gloves and Wildland Gear May 13, 2026 Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email The protective clothing worn by firefighters often contains a class of chemicals called PFAS. Exposure to PFAS, also known as “forever chemicals,” has been linked to negative health outcomes. In the fourth of an ongoing series of reports, NIST shows that wear and tear increased the levels of PFAS found in hoods and gloves, but it decreased the levels found in wildland gear. A firefighter’s protective clothing is composed of three distinct layers made of different textiles. In response to concerns about the gear possibly exposing firefighters to PFAS chemicals — several of which have been linked to cancer — NIST researchers investigated the presence of the chemicals in textiles used to make the layers. This latest study analyzed how wear and tear affects the amount of PFAS in hoods and gloves worn in structural fires as well as protective clothing worn to fight wildfires. Credit: B. And in Nome, warmer winters means lake, river and sea ice that is too thin and weak for safe winter travel. Coastal areas typically have mild weather, while the interior has greater seasonal variation in temperature and precipitation. In Nome, yearly precipitation averages about 15 inches, and the average temperature is about 21 o F. Summers average around 50 o F. The first snow dusting of the year can fall as early as August, although heavy snowfall begins in October and will stay on the ground until May. Winter temperatures typically range from -10 to -20 o F, although it can reach as low as -65 o F, with an even lower windchill factor. With these extreme temperatures, the sea ice in the Bering and Chukchi Sea will freeze up around mid-October and remain frozen until breakup in late-May. The webinars were specific to the different categories of entities regulated under the final rule. The presentations provided during these webinars are available below. Material on this page was updated to reflect changes to the formaldehyde rule requirements following the March 13, 2018 court order and joint stipulation. Learn more about this action and other rule amendments. pages.text: Welcome Baseball Fans! | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Welcome Baseball Fans! If you're a fan of baseball and disability employment, you've come to the right place! At the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Disability Employment Policy (ODEP), we work to increase success for people with disabilities in America's workplaces. This is a goal we share with our Alliance partner the Professional Baseball Athletic Trainers Society (PBATS). Over the years, ODEP and PBATS have collaborated on a number of activities, including the production of several public service announcements (PSAs) featuring former MLB players with disabilities and/or professional baseball athletic trainers from clubs around the country. Among the topics these PSAs address is the importance of helping people stay at or return to work after injury or illness and, most recently, strategies for fostering mental health-friendly workplaces. Please view and share these PSAs and explore our resources for fostering supportive workplaces, for all workers in all types of workplaces—because everyone should be in the game. pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom. Bachelor's degrees typically require about 120 college credits, while associate degrees usually require around 60 credits. A credit hour usually represents about one hour in class and two hours of work outside class each week, which helps determine how much time a course requires. You can earn credits in different ways to help shorten the time it takes to graduate. Learn how college credits are measured and ways you may be able to expedite earning your degree. Acid rain, or acid deposition, is a broad term that includes any form of precipitation with acidic components, such as sulfuric or nitric acid that fall to the ground from the atmosphere in wet or dry forms. This can include rain, snow, fog, hail or even dust that is acidic. What Causes Acid Rain? This image illustrates the pathway for acid rain in our environment: (1) Emissions of SO2 and NOx are released into the air, where (2) the pollutants are transformed into acid particles that may be transported long distances. (3) These acid particles then fall to the earth as wet and dry deposition (dust, rain, snow, etc.) and (4) may cause harmful effects on soil, forests, streams, and lakes. Acid rain results when sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) and nitrogen oxides (NO X ) are emitted into the atmosphere and transported by wind and air currents. The SO 2 and NO X react with water, oxygen and other chemicals to form sulfuric and nitric acids. These then mix with water and other materials before falling to the ground. For centuries, royal figures, government officials and military officers — along with spies and assassins — have used secret codes to protect their confidential messages. These individuals were performing early versions of cryptography — employing mathematical techniques to protect the security of information. These secret codes, known as ciphers, could be as simple as taking a message and shifting each letter of the alphabet by a certain number of positions so that A became D, B became E, etc. But cryptography has evolved greatly since these earliest examples. Nowadays, digital devices such as computers routinely carry out mathematical operations to scramble information in highly complex ways. In addition to being much more technologically advanced, modern cryptography frequently includes authentication — verifying that both the sender and the receiver of information really are who they say they are.
